paras: The Barney shooting and race-riot scare took place on Christmas Day 1903 at Barney, Georgia, a village near Quitman, when a white man, Perry Peeples, shot and killed an unnamed Black man and Black residents were reported to have "took up the fight." The sheriff took an armed posse to the village by special train, found it quiet, and returned the same night. White newspapers in Georgia and beyond headlined the episode as a feared "race riot" among Black residents rather than as a killing.

According to a Quitman dispatch dated December 25, "the trouble started between some whites and black[s]" at Barney, ending when Peeples shot and killed a man the dispatch called "a desperate negro." The dispatch did not say what the dispute was about or who began it. After the Black residents "took up the fight," white citizens at Barney, "apprehensive of trouble," telephoned Quitman for Sheriff Conolly. The sheriff left with "a posse of several armed men" on a special train over the South Georgia road.

A follow-up from Quitman on December 26 reported that the posse "found things quiet" and had come back the night before. Threats made that afternoon, and an interruption of telephone service, had left the authorities uneasy, and they still feared further trouble.

The only arrest effort reported was directed at a Black man: authorities were taking measures "to find and arrest the negro who is attempting to stir up violence." No report of an arrest, inquest or charge against Peeples was found, and the dead man was never named.

The fullest account, a Quitman special in the Savannah Morning News, ran under "Trouble at Barney" and closed by calling the dead man "a bad character, having been only recently released from jail." The Atlanta Constitution printed the same dispatch two days later under "Fear Race Riot Above Quitman," spelling the shooter's name "Perry Peoples" and calling the trouble "a probable race war." Only the Savannah paper carried the follow-up saying the posse had found Barney quiet.

A shorter press-association version, without names, appeared on December 26 in papers from Montgomery to San Francisco, describing "the killing of a negro desperado by a white man" and "excitement among the blacks." Headline writers stressed the threat from Black residents: "Blacks May Break Out" in Phoenix, "Race War Feared" in Indianapolis, "Negros Excited" in Providence and "Whites and Blacks in a Riot in Georgia" in Butte. The San Francisco Call was the exception in heading its version "Murder of Negro Causes Excitement," though its subhead still read "Blacks Threaten an Uprising." Vermont and Kentucky papers reprinted the wire as late as December 28 and 31 under new datelines.
No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

Reports differed on where Barney lay: the Savannah dispatch put it "eighteen miles north" of Quitman, the Atlanta Constitution's identical text "eight miles north," and the wire "eighteen miles east."

reader.title: Barney shooting and race-riot scare
bases: A single named white man shot and killed an unnamed Black man, after which the sheriff took an armed posse to Barney against a feared Black 'riot' that it did not find (A1, A13); no mob action, attack on the posse or second casualty is reported (A13).

Two differently worded Quitman dispatches, the Savannah/Atlanta special (A1, A14) and the press-association wire (A2), agree on the core event, the killing of a Black man by a white man at Barney and the sheriff's posse; both originate in Quitman and no report from Barney itself or from the Black press was found.

accounts.label: Quitman special to Savannah Morning News / Atlanta Constitution
accounts.gist: Trouble between whites and Blacks at Barney ended with Perry Peeples killing a 'desperate negro'; the Black residents 'took up the fight', citizens telephoned for the sheriff, and a posse went by special train. The dead man was a bad character lately out of jail.

accounts.label: Press-association wire from Quitman
accounts.gist: Trouble at the village of Barney grew out of the killing of a 'negro desperado' by a white man; rioting was feared because of 'excitement among the blacks', and the sheriff and a posse had gone to the scene.

accounts.label: Quitman follow-up, Dec. 26
accounts.gist: The posse found Barney quiet and came back; afternoon threats and a cut telephone line had alarmed authorities, who were seeking to arrest a Black man said to be stirring up violence.

framing.detail: The Georgia special labeled the dead man 'a desperate negro' and 'a bad character' recently out of jail, and treated Black residents' response, not the killing, as the threat ('probable riot', 'Fear Race Riot Above Quitman').

Out-of-state papers ran the wire under headlines stressing Black unrest: 'Blacks May Break Out', 'Race War Feared', 'Whites and Blacks in a Riot in Georgia'; the San Francisco Call alone headed it 'Murder of Negro'.

conflicts.note: The Atlanta Constitution prints the same dispatch as Savannah with 'eight' for 'eighteen', likely a typesetting difference; the wire says east.
